title: Post-purchase onboarding: The 7-day sequence that saves the customers most businesses lose
hook: The seven days after a customer buys decides more than any ad you will run next month.
caption:
The seven days after a customer buys decides more than any ad you will run next month.

Most businesses near 100k spend that window on a single welcome email. Then silence. Then a generic newsletter two weeks later. Then a "we miss you" note once they have already gone.

Here is a different seven-day plan. Six emails. One week. It works across products, coaching, and small e-commerce.

Day zero. A welcome from a person, not a brand. One paragraph. Who they have joined. What to expect from you for the next week.

Day one. A small win. One thing they can do with the product today that leaves them with a result they can point at. Not a full tour. One completed step.

Day two. One real story. Two or three sentences from another customer, told in that customer's own words. Not a case study. A quote, a screenshot, a voice note.

Day three. A second thing they can use you for. This is the most important email in the set. When a customer uses you for a second thing inside the first week, they tend to stay.

Day five. A check-in. Not "do you need help." Ask what they tried this week that did not work. A specific question gets a specific answer. A vague one gets silence.

Day seven. A standing time. Suggest a day of the week or a moment in their routine where this fits. You are turning a purchase into a habit.

Six emails, one week. It is not a clever sequence. It is the sequence most businesses skip because it takes an afternoon to write properly.

title: A 7-day onboarding teardown for businesses near 100k
hook: The seven days after a customer buys is the most valuable window you will ever have with them. Most businesses near 100k spend it on one welcome email and then go silent for a fortnight.
tweets:
The seven days after a customer buys is the most valuable window you will ever have with them.

Most businesses near 100k spend it on one welcome email and then go silent for a fortnight.

Here is an email-by-email breakdown of what actually fits in those seven days.

Day zero. One paragraph from a real person, signed by a real name.

Tell them who they have joined and what you will send them this week. No tour. No checklist. A greeting.

Day one. A small win.

Point them at one thing they can do in the product today that ends with something to show. Not the feature list. One finished step. A small win beats a full tour.

Day two. A real story.

Two or three sentences from another customer, in that customer's own words. A quote, a screenshot, a voice note. Not a polished case study. The rough version is what gets read.

Day three. A second use.

Point them at a different thing your product or service also does. A buyer who uses you for a second thing inside the first week stays the longest. Miss this email, lose the customer.

Day five. A specific question.

Ask what they tried that did not work. Not "do you need help." A specific question, in one line. You will get a specific answer.

Day seven. A standing time.

Suggest a day of the week where this fits. Tuesdays after lunch. Sunday evening. You are turning a one-time purchase into a habit.

Six emails, one week. It will not win an award. Writing it properly takes an afternoon.

If the window is empty in your business right now, that is where this quarter's retention work lives.

title: The day zero email that predicts 30-day retention
hook: The first email after a customer buys has three jobs. Most businesses near 100k only do the first.
caption:
The first email after a customer buys has three jobs. Most businesses near 100k only do the first.

Here is a three-section template.

Section one. Welcome. One sentence that names who they have joined. Not "welcome to the product." The group of people this product is for. The name of that group.

Section two. What to expect this week. Three short lines. What you will send them. When it lands. What it asks of them.

Section three. A small first step. Point them at one thing they can do today. End with a line asking them to reply if they want help.

Timing. Send it within one hour of the purchase. Not twelve hours. Not the next morning. One hour. The customer is still in the decision. You want to be there while they are.

title: LI Second Post: Retention does not show up next week
hook: Retention does not show up next week. The first six emails in the first seven days after a customer buys will change your business in roughly ninety days, not seven.
caption:
Retention does not show up next week.

The first six emails in the first seven days after a customer buys will change your business in roughly ninety days, not seven.

Most businesses near 100k try a new ad, a new feature, a new discount, and hope for a difference inside a month. When nothing moves in thirty days, they drop the thing and try the next. Retention work does not show its face that quickly.

Write the six. Send them to every new customer. Do not touch them for three months. Then look at the ninety-day number. That is the number retention speaks in.

title: How to read a competitor's ad like a creative strategist
hook: How to read one of your competitor's ads like a creative strategist. The move that changes your copy more than any course on frameworks.
caption:
How to read one of your competitor's ads like a creative strategist.

Here is the move that changes your copy more than any course on frameworks. Pick one ad from a competitor you would like to work with. Spend twenty minutes on it. Not scrolling. Not screenshotting. Reading.

Four questions.

One. Who is the first line of this ad talking to. Picture the person. Not the category. A specific person. Age, life stage, mood. If you cannot picture them, the ad is not working, you just have not noticed yet.

Two. What does the ad promise that person in the first three seconds. Not the product. The promise. In one sentence.

Three. What did the brand do to make the promise believable. A face on camera. A before and after. A stat. A mechanism. A testimonial. Name the move.

Four. What would you test next, if you ran this account tomorrow. One specific thing. Your hypothesis on the result.

If you do this on four ads this week, your writing gets sharper than another course could make it. You are training your eye to see what a creative strategist is paid to see.

title: How to tear down a winning ad (FB Page)
hook: How to tear down a winning ad when you are trying to become a creative strategist. Every creative strategist has a swipe file. Learning to actually look at an ad is what gets skipped.
caption:
How to tear down a winning ad when you are trying to become a creative strategist.

Every creative strategist has a swipe file somewhere on their laptop. Screenshots, bookmarks, a Notion page that gets long and never reread. The file is the easy part. Learning to actually look at an ad is what gets skipped.

Here are four questions that turn a swipe into a teardown. Run them on every ad you save for the next two weeks.

One. Who is this ad written for. Not the category. The specific person the first line is speaking to. Read the first line out loud. Picture the person. Write one sentence about who that is. Age, life stage, what they were doing when they saw this ad.

Two. What is the promise in the first three seconds. Not what the brand is selling. What the ad is saying it will give the viewer. Name it in one sentence.

Three. What did the brand do to make the promise believable. A face on camera. A before and after. A customer quote. A stat. A mechanism. Name the move.

Four. What would you test next if you ran this account. Not what you would critique. What you would try. One specific change. Your guess on what would happen.

If you answer those four on every ad you save, inside a month you have a folder that looks like a strategy document. You will also find that your own hooks get easier to write.

A creative strategist is hired to answer question four for a living. Start practicing now.

hook: Who is the ad for? Read the first line. Picture the exact person it is talking to.
caption:
Who is the ad for?

Read the first line. Picture the exact person it is talking to. Not the category. Not the age range. The specific human.

If you can picture them in the room, the ad has a chance. If you cannot, the ad is hedging, and a hedging ad never beats a specific one.

The hardest part of creative strategy is picking one person for the first line. The rest of the ad follows.
